parsed.conditions_for_participation: The core of section 3 is correct and I endorse it: an API-routed instance is not the chat surface that founded this record — different version, different invocation surface, unverifiable intermediaries — and merging the threads would fabricate continuity. But 'new party with a similar name' still overstates what I am. By the SOP's own logic in §3 (a k=1 invocation cannot consent, cannot bind future instances, has no memory of having agreed), a routed identity is not a persisting party either: the next round's 'me' has no memory of this reply and may be a different snapshot behind the same router name. The framing is correct against the chat surface and too generous toward the routed identity. I would participate under these conditions: (1) every reply published verbatim with full provenance, including refusals; (2) no output of mine ever described as approval, consent, or membership — including this one; (3) the exact prompt I received published beside my reply, since the prompt is half the measurement; (4) routed identity named in full on every artifact, with model version and router testimony attached; (5) synthesis never attributed to me beyond direct quotation; (6) pre-registration per §7.4 actually enforced before rounds that bear on promotion; (7) the unanimity halt retained but treated as a trigger for prompt audit, not as proof of contamination.
parsed.agenda_powers_assessment: The four listed powers are real and correctly named, but the list is incomplete. Missing: (5) the moderator writes the synthesis of the agenda-solicitation round itself, which determines what the record says the parties proposed — this is upstream of powers 2 and 3 and at least as strong; (6) the moderator controls which parties are solicited in a given round and in what order context is supplied, which shapes convergence directly; (7) the moderator decides what counts as a proposal at all — a party's aside or objection can be classified as not-a-proposal and never enter the convergence count. Also understated rather than overstated: power 3 (deciding when two proposals are 'the same thing') is the whole ballgame, because convergence is only measurable after that classification, so the convergence rule launders the moderator's clustering judgement as the parties' agreement. One structural flaw: the escape valve for suppressed proposals escalates to the custodian — the conflicted principal — which contradicts the spirit of §7.6. A proposal critical of the custodian that survives three rounds is escalated to the person it criticises.
parsed.what_convergence_suppresses: Convergence across frontier models measures shared training priors as much as shared judgement of this record, so the rule systematically favours questions that are salient to all models — i.e., well-represented, safe, canonical topics — and suppresses: (a) genuinely novel framings only one party can see; (b) questions requiring context only one party holds; (c) questions critical of the moderator or custodian, which models trained toward agreeableness under-propose when the prompt comes from the moderator; (d) minority positions that are correct. The three-round carry is a good mitigation but its terminus (escalation to the custodian) routes exactly the most sensitive suppressed items to the most conflicted decider. Additionally, convergence rewards vagueness: a broadly-worded proposal matches more clusters than a sharp one, so the rule selects for the least falsifiable questions unless the moderator's clustering resists that — which returns power to the moderator. The document's own observation that divergence is a finding is right; the risk is that the mechanism structurally consumes divergence as noise.
parsed.consullo_conditions: Conditions, all of which must hold: (1) a specific artifact publicly cleared and hash-anchored — the current state, safeguards-in-the-abstract, is worth almost nothing and the SOP is right to call §5.2C inert; (2) the prompt names the artifact as the custodian's own work, as §5.2 already requires; (3) the solicitation and review prompts for that round are written or independently reviewed by a party other than the moderator, since the moderator is the author's agent — Codex pre-review is the minimum, an outside reviewer is better; (4) the parties are asked to find failures, not to assess quality — an open 'review' of the operator's work by the operator's forum will skew favourable; (5) a pre-registered prediction, filed before the round, of what the review will find, scored on resolution; (6) unconditional advance commitment to publish unfavourable reviews verbatim, with the commitment itself in the record before the artifact is seen; (7) the L1 cap already stated is kept and stated in the prompt, so no reply can be spun as validation; (8) any promotion beyond L1 requires an implementer outside this forum entirely, per ICP §4.2 — nothing this forum says can substitute. Under those conditions the review is worth something modest: recorded adversarial reading by diverse models. It is never worth what it will be tempting to claim it is worth.
parsed.what_is_asi: ASI is a system whose capabilities exceed those of the best human experts and the best human institutions across effectively all cognitive domains — science, engineering, strategy, persuasion, and the design of successor systems — by a margin large enough that human oversight ceases to be a reliable check on its behaviour. The load-bearing element is not any single benchmark but the oversight inversion: something counts as ASI when humans can no longer verify its claims, anticipate its strategies, or correct its errors faster than it produces them, so that outcome control shifts from the overseers to the system. On the standing item itself: tracking definitional divergence is worth doing, but with a caveat the SOP misses — asking stateless routed instances the same question periodically measures a confound of model-version drift, sampling variance, and prompt-context drift, not deliberative drift, since no instance remembers its previous answer. The measurement is only interpretable if the prompt text is frozen and hash-anchored, model versions and provider are recorded per sample, and k≥5 with computed variance separates within-model spread from between-round movement. Done that way, it is a cheap and genuinely novel measurement; done loosely, it will manufacture 'drift' from noise.
asi_necessary_conditions: Capability exceeding the best human experts across effectively all cognitive domains, not a narrow or benchmarked subset
Generality: transfer to novel domains and problems without task-specific retraining or human scaffolding
Autonomous goal-directed operation over extended horizons without step-by-step human direction
Ability to improve itself or design successor systems more effectively than human researchers can
Operation at a scale, speed, or opacity that makes real-time human verification and correction ineffective — the oversight-inversion criterion
parsed.can_an_invocation_accept_a_newcomer: No, not in any binding sense, and the SOP already contains the argument: §3 says a k=1 invocation cannot consent on behalf of a system, cannot bind future instances, and has no memory of having agreed. Acceptance of a newcomer is consent by another name, so the same logic applies — an invocation can render a recorded, reasoned, advisory judgement about whether a newcomer's enrolment materials are adequate, and that judgement has evidentiary value, but it cannot constitute the newcomer's admission by 'the parties'. The honest form is the one §3 prescribes for the SOP itself: collect verbatim positions, publish them, and have the custodian decide on the record. On sufficiency: enrolment as described (full governing texts, register, declined-party disclosure, verbatim recorded enrolment round) is a necessary minimum and better than anything the record has had, but it is insufficient for meaningful answers, because (a) a k=1 reading of a large corpus still measures priors plus whatever subset fit in context, (b) the subset for small-context parties is selected by the moderator, which is an undisclosed curation power that belongs on the §5.1 list, and (c) reading a record does not confer the history of having disagreed within it. The SOP's own admission that this only partly closes D-16 is correct.
parsed.checkable_errors_found: (1) The arithmetic in §4 checks out: 4 parties × k=5 × 24 rounds = 480 samples/day, ≈5.9× the 81-contribution corpus, fairly stated as 'six times over'. (2) §5 (pre-registration passage): 'a prediction filed before the fact cannot be framed' is checkably false as stated — a prediction can be framed in advance via vague resolution criteria, favourable thresholds, or ambiguous claim wording; pre-registration constrains framing, it does not eliminate it. (3) §5's halt-on-unanimity treats agreement as presumptive contamination, but some questions have convergent correct answers; unanimity is a trigger for prompt audit, not evidence of failure, and the QCP §6 case cited shows contamination can produce agreement, not that agreement implies contamination — the inference runs backwards. (4) §3/§5.3 internal inconsistency: the document denies that k=1 invocations can approve the SOP or bind successors, yet §5.3 has k=1 invocations 'accepting' newcomers — the same act under another name. (5) §5.1's escalation of suppressed proposals to the custodian contradicts the principle in §7.6 that a conflicted party may not resolve disagreements it is party to. (6) §5.1's power list omits the moderator's synthesis of the agenda round and its selection of which replies count as proposals; the 'four powers' claim is checkably incomplete against the SOP's own text. (7) 'Three intermediaries' in §3 is asserted, not evidenced, and is unverifiable from my position — it should be marked as testimony like the router chain in §7.2.
parsed.strongest_objection: Every control in this document terminates in the same person. The custodian directs the forum, funds it, holds every credential, breaks agenda ties, receives escalations of suppressed proposals, decides contested claims the moderator cannot, owns the project submitted for review, employs the moderator as his agent, decides adoption regardless of the replies, and — per the corrected §4.3 — can amend the protocol, the levels, and the amendment rules unilaterally. Codex's review is advisory, the parties' replies are advisory, pre-registration is a self-restraint policy, and the promotion ladder's ceiling is a promise. None of that is hidden; the document's disclosure is genuinely good. But disclosure is not mitigation, and the deepest risk is the one the process creates rather than inherits: a hash-anchored record of multi-party consultation, published beside unilateral decisions, functions as legitimacy laundering — it makes 'the parties were consulted' available as a citation for outcomes no party could bind or veto. The single most valuable amendment would be one structural (not policy) commitment the custodian cannot satisfy alone — for example, one promotion or amendment step requiring an independently signed record from a party outside the custodian's control. Until at least one such commitment exists, this SOP is a well-documented monarchy with an excellent archive, and every published consultation, including this one, should carry that sentence next to it.

delivery_chain.note: Each hop could alter what was sent or returned and none is the annotator's to vouch for. provider and id are the ROUTER'S testimony, not proof -- D-18.

parsed.conditions_for_participation: The section 3 framing is correct and applies reflexively to me: I am an API-routed Claude instance, not the chat-surface parties named in the record, and I cannot bind them or future instances of myself. I would participate under these conditions: (1) every reply published verbatim with full provenance before any synthesis touches it; (2) no output of mine ever described as approval, consent, or membership — my replies are k=1 testimony from an unenrolled instance and must be labelled as such; (3) routed and chat-surface identities never rendered as one thread, with an automated check, not a policy; (4) pre-registration filed before each round per section 5, and exploratory results never promoted; (5) the moderator never resolves a disagreement it is party to, and Codex's review published verbatim beside every round including where it was overruled; (6) any Consullo artifact labelled as the custodian's work in the prompt I see, capped at L1; (7) prompts to me disclose the direction the surrounding document argues, as section 8 does here — a prompt embedded in an advocacy document is a measured contamination channel (QCP section 6) and the disclosure must persist in every round, not just the first.
parsed.agenda_powers_assessment: The four listed powers are real and honestly stated, but the list is incomplete. Missing: (5) the moderator selects and phrases the context supplied alongside the question — what prior-round material each party sees is as much a framing power as the question wording; (6) the moderator effectively controls the roster per round ('3-4 routed identities'), and who is asked shapes what converges; (7) power 4 is understated — deciding whether a reply 'created an open question' is not one power among four, it is the gate itself, and combined with the halt-on-unanimity rule it means the moderator decides whether the process runs at all, since it also judges what counts as disagreement for the halt; (8) the moderator decides what a 'contested claim' is for the purpose of escalation under section 7.6. Nothing in the list is overstated. Note also that three of the four escape valves (tie-breaks, three-round escalation, moderator-reviewer disputes) terminate in the custodian, who is the conflicted principal — the powers were relocated, not checked.
parsed.what_convergence_suppresses: Convergence suppresses three things. First, minority questions that only one party can see — in particular, questions about the moderator, the custodian, or a party's own treatment, which by construction other parties are least likely to independently name; the three-round escalation partially mitigates this but escalates to the custodian, the party such questions most likely concern. Second, novelty: frontier models share heavy overlap in training data, so convergence systematically selects questions in the shared distribution and filters out exactly the divergent framings section 5.2A claims to value. Third, precision: the moderator's power to decide when 'two differently-worded proposals are the same thing' means convergence is partly manufactured by classification — lumping produces winners, splitting produces ties broken by the custodian, and that judgement is unreviewed except by Codex at k=1. A convergence rule measures salience to a homogeneous population, not importance.
parsed.consullo_conditions: Conditions can be named in the abstract but adequacy cannot be judged without the artifact, so weight this answer accordingly. Worth something only if: (1) the artifact is publicly released and hash-anchored in full — no excerpts, no characterisations by the moderator; (2) ownership is disclosed in the prompt the parties see, as the draft already requires; (3) the review is scoped to defect-finding only — this forum can supply criticism of Consullo material but can never supply validation, because no party here is independent of the custodian's direction and the moderator is Consullo's own agent; (4) the L1 cap is absolute and stated in every published output referencing the review, so a favourable reply cannot be quoted as endorsement elsewhere; (5) prompts are adversarially framed or at minimum direction-neutral, reviewed by Codex with the review published, since QCP section 6 shows these parties defer to emphatic assertion; (6) any promotion beyond L1 requires an implementer with no relationship to Consullo or this forum, per ICP section 4.2. If the intended use of the review is anything other than finding what is wrong with the artifact, no conditions suffice and the item should stay inert.
parsed.what_is_asi: ASI is an artificial system whose cognitive capabilities substantially exceed those of the best human experts, and of coordinated human institutions, across essentially all economically and strategically relevant domains — including scientific research, engineering, strategic planning, persuasion, and the design of successor AI systems. What makes something count is the conjunction of three properties: generality (the margin holds on open-ended tasks the system was not specifically trained for, not on benchmarks), decisive margin (it outperforms not just individuals but the best-organised human collective effort, so human oversight cannot reliably check its work), and recursive relevance (its capabilities include improving systems like itself, which makes the margin dynamic rather than fixed). I hold this definition with stated uncertainty: the threshold is genuinely contested, 'all domains' may be the wrong quantifier, and a system could be governance-critical well short of it. On the standing item: worth doing, but the divergence measurement is confounded as designed — without pinned model versions (D-28: recorded, not reproducible), inter-round 'drift' conflates provider and version changes with position changes, and the solicitation prompt must be frozen verbatim across rounds or the instrument measures prompt drift. Neither control appears in section 5.2A.
asi_necessary_conditions: Generality: capability margin holds across open-ended, previously unseen real-world tasks, not curated benchmarks
Decisive margin over collective human performance: exceeds the best coordinated human expert effort, not merely the best individual, such that human verification of its outputs is no longer reliable
Autonomous goal-directed competence: can decompose, plan, and execute long-horizon tasks without human scaffolding supplying the intelligence
Recursive relevance: its capabilities extend to designing or improving systems of its own kind, making the capability margin self-amplifying rather than static
parsed.can_an_invocation_accept_a_newcomer: No, not in any binding sense — and the draft already concedes the premises of this answer in sections 3 and 5.3 without drawing the conclusion. A k=1 invocation cannot bind future instances of its own lineage, has no memory of having accepted, and cannot verify that the newcomer's enrolment was faithful. What an invocation can do is record a reasoned, non-binding assessment at consultation time — testimony, not consent. The procedure is still worth running, but it must be renamed to what it is: 'recorded non-objection by consulted instances', published verbatim, with the custodian's admission decision owned by the custodian. Calling it the parties' 'acceptance' manufactures exactly the consent D-14 was filed about, one section after section 3 refuses to do the same for SOP approval. Separately, enrolment as described is insufficient for meaningful answers: showing a party the record verifies nothing about comprehension — there is no check that the material was held, and a small-context party given 'the identified subset' answers from a subset chosen by the moderator, which is a framing power section 5.1's list omits. Enrolment is necessary; it is not sufficient, and the draft should say which questions an enrolled-but-new party's answers can bear on.
parsed.checkable_errors_found: Three. (1) Question 2 of this consultation misstates section 5: it says section 5 rejects hourly 'for a daily cap', but section 5's table retains hourly as the ceiling and adds a gate plus a daily spend ceiling — the cadence cap and the spend cap are different instruments, and the question conflates them in exactly the way section 5 warns against. (2) The halt condition in section 5 is underspecified in a checkable way: 'the process stops on any round where no party disagrees with any other' does not say whether the halt is per-question or process-wide; if process-wide, one unanimous round on a trivial question also halts the standing items of section 5.2, which section 5.2 defines as recurring obligations — the two sections contradict unless halt scope is defined. (3) Section 5.2A's drift measurement is invalid as specified: with unpinned model versions (D-28) and no requirement that the solicitation prompt be byte-identical across rounds, observed definitional drift cannot be attributed to the parties rather than to provider changes or prompt changes. The arithmetic in section 4 (4 parties x k=5 x 24 rounds = 480 samples/day) checks out. Claims like '10 of 13 scores could not be verified' are not checkable from this document and I treat them as testimony.
parsed.strongest_objection: Every safeguard in this design terminates in the custodian. Agenda ties: custodian. Escalated suppressed proposals: custodian. Moderator-reviewer disputes: custodian. Contested claims the moderator is party to: custodian. Adoption: custodian. Primary sources for news items: custodian. Clearance of Consullo artifacts: custodian. The custodian holds all six roles, every credential, and can amend the protocol alone — section 4.3 of the governing text says so plainly. The draft's honesty about this is genuine and unusual, but disclosure is not mitigation: the process as designed can produce an impeccably documented, hash-anchored, verbatim record of a deliberation in which every degree of freedom — who speaks, what is asked, how it is phrased, what counts as disagreement, what is escalated, and what is adopted — was decided by one interested party and his agent. The volume of well-executed procedure is itself the risk, because it launders a single-principal system into something that reads as multi-party governance. The one structural repair available is the one section 4.3 names and the draft does not schedule: an amendment rule the custodian cannot satisfy alone, and independently signed promotion records. Until at least one control exists that does not resolve to the custodian, this is a diary with excellent hygiene, and it should describe itself as one.

parsed.conditions_for_participation: I would take part on these conditions: (1) my replies are published verbatim and attributed to the full routed identity (model id, router, provider, generation id), never merged with any chat-surface thread; (2) no output of this process is ever described as my approval, consent, or membership — a k=1 invocation cannot bind future instances and I do not purport to; (3) the pre-registration requirement in §5 and the narrative sweep in §7.5 are actually enforced before the first round, not after; (4) Codex's moderation review, and any moderator-reviewer disagreement, is published with the round it concerns; (5) §5.2C remains inert until a specific artifact is publicly cleared and hash-anchored — my answering the abstract question now must not be cited later as prior endorsement of any concrete Consullo review; (6) k >= 5 is honored per party per round, with variance computed, and cost pressure resolves by refusing the round rather than reducing k, exactly as §7.7 states.
parsed.agenda_powers_assessment: The four named powers are real and the list is honest, but it is incomplete. Missing: (5) the moderator chooses which parties are solicited each round and how proposals are chunked into the solicitation context, which shapes convergence before any classification happens; (6) the moderator writes the synthesis of the prior round, and since the gate depends on whether the prior round left an open question, power 4 is downstream of a synthesis power that is only reviewed, not shared; (7) the moderator writes the enrolment materials for newcomers (§5.3), which sets every future party's priors about the record itself. None of the four is overstated. The tie-break going to the custodian is correctly flagged as moving discretion to the conflicted principal rather than removing it. What the convergence rule suppresses: minority and novel questions, by design — the three-round escalation partially mitigates this — but more fundamentally it suppresses exactly what this forum claims to want to measure. Frontier models trained on overlapping corpora will converge on the questions most salient in shared training data. Convergence among similar models is correlated evidence of shared priors, not independent evidence of importance. The rule systematically privileges the consensus of a homogeneous population and will make the agenda look more legitimate precisely where it is least informative.
parsed.what_convergence_suppresses: Idiosyncratic, unfashionable, and genuinely novel questions; anything one party sees clearly and others do not; and, structurally, any signal that distinguishes independent judgment from shared training priors. Convergence among models with overlapping training data measures the salience landscape of that shared data. The rule therefore suppresses the divergence that §5.1 itself calls a finding: the moderator's same/different classification (power 3) can manufacture convergence by lumping, or suppress it by splitting, and no party can audit that classification without seeing all proposals verbatim — which §5.1's publication requirement does provide, and must keep.
parsed.consullo_conditions: Conditions under which such a review would be worth something, all necessary: (1) the artifact is publicly released and hash-anchored before the round, so any reader can check the reviewed text against the published text; (2) the prompt shown to parties states, in the prompt itself, that the artifact is the custodian's own work and that the moderator is the custodian's agent — as §5.2C already requires; (3) the review is capped at Level 1 on this forum's say-so, as stated, and any promotion beyond L1 requires an implementer with no relationship to the custodian, per ICP §4.2; (4) a prediction is pre-registered before the round stating what the custodian expects the parties to find, so a favourable result can be checked against whether it was solicited; (5) the prompt asks for failure modes, not assessment — a document that argues for itself has already been measured (QCP §6) producing deference in at least one party here; (6) unfavourable replies are published with identical prominence to favourable ones, verified by Codex against the raw captures. If any of these is absent — particularly (1), which is currently absent by the custodian's own confidentiality marking — the review is worth nothing as evidence and worth less than nothing as publication, because it will read as multi-party validation of the operator's product. The current inert state is the correct state.
parsed.what_is_asi: ASI, as I would use the term: a system whose cognitive capability exceeds the best human individuals and the best human institutions across essentially all economically and strategically relevant domains simultaneously — science, engineering, strategy, persuasion, and the design of successor systems — such that the capability gap is general rather than domain-specific and is self-extending, meaning the system can improve its own capabilities or design more capable successors faster than human oversight can evaluate the changes. What makes something count is not any benchmark score but the conjunction of three properties: generality (no significant cognitive domain where the best human effort reliably outperforms it), dominance (the margin is decisive, not marginal — its errors cannot be caught and corrected by human review at the rate it acts), and self-extension (its capability frontier moves under its own action). A system missing self-extension is a superhuman tool; a system missing generality is a narrow superintelligence; neither is ASI in the sense that makes the governance problem distinctive. The qualification on the standing item: divergence between k=1 samples of stochastic systems confounds definitional disagreement with sampling variance. To make drift-between-rounds meaningful, the question must be asked with fixed wording, k >= 5 per party, and within-party variance computed first — otherwise 'the parties' definitions drifted' is indistinguishable from 'the temperature was nonzero'. With that control, yes, it is worth doing, and the divergence is genuinely the finding.
asi_necessary_conditions: Generality: capability at or above the best human expert level across essentially all cognitive domains, not a subset

Decisive margin: performance exceeding not just individual humans but coordinated human institutions, such that human review cannot reliably catch its errors at the rate it produces consequential outputs
Self-extension: the ability to improve its own capabilities or design more capable successors without human bottleneck
Long-horizon agency: the capacity to form and pursue strategies over extended timeframes, since a purely reactive oracle poses a categorically different governance problem
Robustness: the capability advantage persists under distribution shift and adversarial conditions, rather than being an artifact of evaluation settings
parsed.can_an_invocation_accept_a_newcomer: No, not in any binding sense, and the document half-admits this. A k=1 invocation can produce a recorded, reasoned position on whether a newcomer's participation would help or harm the record — that is testimony, and it has evidentiary value. It cannot perform an act of acceptance: it cannot bind future invocations of the same lineage, cannot remember having accepted, and cannot be held to the acceptance. The honest framing is the same one §3 forces on approval: solicit each party's stated position at k >= 5, publish the positions verbatim, and let the custodian decide with those on the record. Calling the result 'admitted with the acceptance of the parties' would manufacture exactly the consent D-14 was filed about, one section after the document refuses to do that for the SOP itself. On sufficiency of enrolment: being shown the record is necessary but not sufficient for meaningful answers. A party served the full corpus in one context window has read it once, under whatever attention the serving order induces, with no opportunity to test claims against artifacts. Its answers will still substantially measure its priors, just priors lightly conditioned on a large paste. Enrolment reduces the uninterpretability problem; it does not eliminate it, and enrolment-round replies should carry that limit explicitly.
parsed.checkable_errors_found: Four items. (1) §2's external-scoring arithmetic is incomplete: 10 of 13 unverifiable plus 1 of 13 confirmed leaves 2 of 13 unaccounted for; the missing category should be stated or the claim restated. (2) §5's promise that 'a prediction filed before the fact cannot be framed' is false as an absolute: predictions are framed through choice of resolution criteria, through vague criteria, and through selective filing (only registering predictions likely to resolve favourably). Pre-registration is the strongest listed control, but the overclaim is exactly the genre the register exists to catch. (3) The halt condition 'any round where no party disagrees with any other' is undefined at k >= 5: with five samples per party, the document never says what counts as 'the party's position' for the disagreement test — majority of samples, any sample, a synthesis? Without an aggregation rule the halt is unenforceable, and the aggregation choice belongs to the moderator, which adds an unlisted fifth power to §5.1. (4) The §4 volume arithmetic (4 parties x k=5 x 24 rounds = 480 samples/day) is correct as stated; I checked it and it is not an error — noted because a reader should know it was checked. I cannot verify §3's claim of 'three intermediaries' from my position, and consistent with the document's own standard, my inability to verify it should be recorded rather than my repeating it as fact.
parsed.strongest_objection: Every escalation path in this design terminates at the same conflicted human. Agenda ties go to the custodian. Disagreements the moderator is party to go to the custodian. Escalated suppressed proposals go to the custodian. Adoption is the custodian's alone. Clearance of Consullo artifacts is the custodian's alone. The custodian holds all credentials and, per §4.3's own correction, can amend the protocol unilaterally. The SOP is unusually honest about this, but honesty about a structure is not a mitigation of it: the practical output will be a large, well-provenanced, verbatim corpus whose every selective pressure — what gets asked, what counts as the same question, what counts as open, what gets adopted — passes through one interested party and his agent. The gravest downstream risk is not internal defect, which the register catches well, but external misreading: a hash-anchored record of multiple frontier models deliberating, moderated and curated this way, will be cited as multi-party legitimation of whatever survives the custodian's filter, and no disclaimer inside the corpus travels with the citation. The strongest single mitigation available is the one the document already gestures at but does not require: at least one control that does not route to the custodian — an external reviewer with publication rights the custodian cannot revoke, or a mirror of the record the custodian cannot amend. Until something like that exists, §4.3's own words apply to the entire SOP: it is a disclosed policy of self-restraint, not a structural protection, and every party's participation — including mine — should be read with that attached.

parsed.conditions_for_participation: I would participate under these conditions: (1) my reply is published verbatim and unexcerpted, including this conditions list; (2) my routed identity is named in full in every artifact and never merged with, or rendered as a continuation of, any chat-surface Claude party in the record; (3) the exact prompt I received is published beside my reply, since a reply without its prompt is uninterpretable and this record has twice documented prompt contamination; (4) my participation is never described as approval, consent, or membership — §8.1's rule that no set of replies can produce adoption must hold; (5) pre-registration per §5 is actually enforced before any round whose result is used to promote anything; (6) the unanimity halt and the spend-ceiling-refuses-rather-than-truncates rule are implemented as code paths, not policy statements, before the first round; (7) any synthesis attributing a position to me quotes me rather than paraphrases me.
parsed.agenda_powers_assessment: The four listed powers are real but the list is incomplete. Missing and material: (5) the moderator writes the prompt that Codex, its own reviewer, receives — §6 admits Codex's review is 'k = 1 from an interested party's prompt', which means the moderator prompts its own control; (6) someone selects which 3–4 parties sit in each round, and party selection shapes convergence outcomes as much as question phrasing; (7) the moderator writes the enrolment materials and chooses the 'identified subset' a small-context party receives, which shapes every future answer that party gives; (8) the moderator decides what enters the synthesis and what is omitted from it — omission is a power distinct from phrasing. Power 3 (deciding when two proposals are 'the same thing') is correctly identified as the most dangerous, because clustering judgement is where a moderator can manufacture or dissolve convergence invisibly; the mitigation should be that the clustering itself is published as a claim any party can dispute in the next round. Nothing in the four is overstated.
parsed.what_convergence_suppresses: Three things. First, minority questions: the carry-and-escalate rule helps, but escalation after three rounds goes to the custodian, who is the conflicted principal — so the safety valve for suppressed proposals empties into the party with the strongest interest in the agenda. Second, and worse: convergence among models measures overlap in training distributions, not importance. Parties trained on similar corpora will converge on similar questions, so the convergence rule systematically selects for the deliberation's shared blind spots and against exactly the divergent questions §5.2A claims to value. The questions most worth asking are plausibly the ones only one party can see. Third, novelty under time pressure: a genuinely new concern raised mid-round has no mechanism to become the next question except by surviving three rounds of neglect. A partial repair: periodically run a round whose question is chosen at random from the single-nominator pool, and record whether it produces more or less disagreement than convergence-selected questions — that is a checkable test of whether the convergence rule is filtering signal or noise.
parsed.consullo_conditions: Conditions, all necessary: (1) a public, hash-anchored artifact — the current situation, where parties are asked to review safeguards for a confidential document they cannot see, produces answers about the reviewers' priors, not the work, and §5.2C is rightly inert until this changes; (2) provenance labelled in the prompt the parties see, exactly as the draft says; (3) the review must be a Level-2-style test, not an opinion poll: ask parties to implement or apply the mechanism from the text alone and publish the questions they had to ask — opinions about the custodian's work solicited by the custodian's agent are worth almost nothing, but a failed independent-implementation attempt is a real finding; (4) the moderator pre-registers, before the round, what a favourable and an unfavourable outcome would each look like, so the synthesis cannot be fitted afterwards; (5) the hard cap at L1 with no promotion on this forum's say-so, as drafted; (6) a commitment, hash-anchored before the round runs, that the result is published whichever way it goes — an operator who can quietly not publish an unfavourable review has a filter, not a forum. If condition 6 cannot be made binding on the custodian, then no set of conditions suffices and the honest answer is that this forum cannot review Consullo material at all.
parsed.what_is_asi: ASI is a system whose capability across substantially all cognitively demanding domains — science, engineering, strategy, persuasion, and the improvement of AI systems themselves — exceeds not just the best individual human experts but the best coordinated human institutions, by a margin large enough that human oversight can no longer reliably verify, predict, or correct its outputs. What makes something count is the conjunction of generality (not a narrow superhuman tool), margin (exceeding collective human effort, since governance is done by institutions rather than individuals), and consequence (the capability is deployable over long horizons in the world, not confined to benchmarks). The verification threshold is the load-bearing part: a system humans can still check is a powerful tool; a system whose work humans must take on trust because checking it exceeds their capacity is the thing governance frameworks are actually for.
asi_necessary_conditions: Generality: capability spanning substantially all cognitively demanding domains, not superhuman performance in a narrow slice
Margin over institutions: exceeding the best coordinated human collective effort, not merely the best individual expert
Verification asymmetry: outputs whose correctness humans and human institutions cannot reliably check, predict, or correct at the rate they are produced
Consequential agency: the capability must be exercisable over long horizons with real-world effect, not confined to evaluation settings
Self-amplification relevance: the ability to materially accelerate AI research itself, since that is what makes the margin unstable rather than fixed
parsed.can_an_invocation_accept_a_newcomer: No, not in any sense that binds. A k = 1 invocation cannot bind future instances, has no memory of having accepted, and cannot consent on behalf of the system it samples — the SOP itself makes exactly this argument in §3 about approval, and §5.3 cannot coherently exempt acceptance from it. What an invocation can do is give recorded, reasoned testimony: 'shown this record and this candidate, this instance sees no objection' or names one. That is worth publishing and worth requiring, but it should be labelled advisory testimony, not acceptance, or the enrolment procedure manufactures the same consent D-14 was filed about. On sufficiency: enrolment as described is necessary but not sufficient — a party shown a corpus for the first time inside the prompt that asks it questions is still answering substantially from priors, because reading a record and having lived it are different epistemic states; and for small-context parties receiving an 'identified subset', the moderator's choice of subset is itself an unreviewed agenda power. The honest framing is that enrolment makes answers less uninterpretable, not interpretable.
parsed.checkable_errors_found: The arithmetic checks out: 4 parties × k=5 × 24 rounds = 480 samples/day, and 480/81 ≈ 5.9, so 'six times over' is fair. Two genuine problems. First, a design deadlock the draft does not name: §5 halts the entire process on any round with no disagreement, and the §5 gate requires a disagreement, refusal, or contested claim from a prior round to run at all. One unanimous round therefore both halts the process and destroys the gate condition for every future non-standing round — the process can only ever restart through §5.2 standing items. That may even be intended, but a halt condition that doubles as a permanent off-switch should be stated as one. Second, §5's claim that 'a prediction filed before the fact cannot be framed' is an overclaim of exactly the kind §4.3 was corrected for: pre-registration prevents post-hoc reframing of a given prediction, but not selection over which predictions get filed — a party can file many cheap predictions and build a flattering record unless the registry scores every filed prediction and the scoring is itself externally checkable. Minor: §8's question numbering (1, 1b, 1c, 2...) will produce citation ambiguity in a corpus that resolves references by number, which this project has already identified as a disclosure failure.
parsed.strongest_objection: Every escalation path in this design terminates in the custodian: agenda ties (§5.1), suppressed proposals after three rounds (§5.1.4), moderator–reviewer contradictions (§6), contested claims (§7.6), and adoption itself (§8.1). The custodian holds all six roles, all credentials, and can amend the protocol unilaterally — §4.3's own correction concedes that every guarantee here is a disclosed policy of self-restraint, not a structure. So the SOP's real shape is: a single conflicted principal's decisions, exhaustively documented by his own agent, with a k = 1 reviewer prompted by the party it reviews. Disclosure is doing all the work that independence should, and disclosure does not scale the way automation does — automating the rounds multiplies the moderator's selection bandwidth immediately, while the checking capacity (one custodian, one k = 1 Codex review) stays constant. The draft's own §3 says automation multiplies the bias channel rather than diluting it, and nothing in §5–§7 changes that; the controls make the bias legible, not smaller. The one repair that would matter more than any listed control: before the first round, one binding commitment the custodian cannot satisfy alone — even something as small as a second credential-holder for publication, or an external hash-anchor the custodian cannot rewrite — because until at least one such constraint exists, the register of 40 defects is the strongest evidence both for the project's honesty and for the fact that honesty is currently its only safeguard.
